steps.title: Combining two tables on a shared key
steps.lede: The customers table holds names; the orders table holds delivery times. To see both together, you join them.

blocks.text: QuickCart stores customer names in a customers table and delivery times in a separate orders table. Each orders row carries a customer_id that points back to customers. To see a customer's name alongside their delivery times, you need both tables combined into one result — that's what a JOIN does.

For each row of T1, an INNER JOIN produces a joined row for each row of T2 that satisfies the join condition; rows from either table with no match are dropped. The query SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id pairs every customer row with every order row that shares its customer_id.

The join condition goes in an ON clause — a boolean expression like those used in WHERE — or in a USING clause when both tables share the same column name. ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id can be written USING (customer_id) when the column name is identical in both tables. INNER is the default: writing JOIN alone, without LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL, already means an INNER JOIN.

steps.title: Unmatched rows disappear
steps.lede: An inner join is strict: if one side has no match, that row is gone.

blocks.text: Because it's an inner join, a customer with zero orders — like customer_id 4 (Chidi Eze), who has no row in orders — produces no row at all in the result. Only customers who have at least one matching order appear.

steps.title: Which rows survive an INNER JOIN?

public.prompt: The **customers** table has rows for customer_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. The **orders** table has rows for customer_id 1, 2, and 3 only. How many distinct customers appear in the result of `SELECT * FROM customers JOIN orders ON customers.customer_id = orders.customer_id`?

options.text: 5 — all customers appear
3 — only customers who have at least one order
2 — only customers who have more than one order
0 — an INNER JOIN always returns an empty result when tables differ in size

opt_a.message: An INNER JOIN drops rows with no match on the other side. Customers 4, 5, and 6 have no orders, so they are excluded.

opt_b.message: Correct. An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that have a match on both sides. Customers 4, 5, and 6 have no matching order rows, so they are dropped.

opt_c.message: The join condition is about matching on customer_id, not about how many orders a customer has. Any customer with at least one order produces at least one joined row.

opt_d.message: An INNER JOIN returns rows whenever a match exists — it does not require the tables to be the same size.

correct.message: An INNER JOIN produces a row only when both sides have a match. Rows with no counterpart on either side are silently dropped.

incorrect.message: Remember: an INNER JOIN keeps only rows that satisfy the join condition on both sides. Any row with no match is dropped.

hints: Think about what happens to a customer who has placed zero orders — does the join condition ever become true for that customer?
The rule is symmetric: a row survives only if both sides have a match.

public.prompt: QuickCart wants to see each order alongside the customer's name. Write a query that joins **customers** to **orders** on `customer_id` and returns the columns **name**, **order_id**, and **delivery_time_minutes**, ordered by `order_id` ascending. Use `JOIN` (or `INNER JOIN`) with an `ON` clause.

files.content:
-- customers columns: customer_id, name, city
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Write a JOIN query that returns name, order_id, delivery_time_minutes
-- ordered by order_id.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.delivery_time_minutes
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return name, order_id, and delivery_time_minutes for every order that has a matching customer, ordered by order_id. Check your JOIN condition and column list.

correct.message: Your INNER JOIN correctly links each order to its customer. Only orders with a matching customer_id appear — rows with no match on either side are dropped.

incorrect.message: Check that you are joining on customer_id, selecting name, order_id, and delivery_time_minutes, and ordering by order_id.

hints: The ON clause should compare the customer_id column from both tables: `ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id`.
Give each table a short alias (e.g. `c` and `o`) so you can qualify columns like `c.name` and `o.order_id`.

steps.title: Joining on two columns at once
steps.lede: When a single column isn't enough to uniquely identify a match, you extend ON with AND.

blocks.text: The shipments table records, for each order_id and product_id pair, the date that item actually shipped. Matching shipments to order_items now needs two columns to agree at once — order_id alone isn't enough, because the same order can contain multiple products.

The ON clause takes a boolean expression of the same kind used in WHERE, so several column-equality tests can be combined with AND to require all of them to match before rows join. FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id joins a shipment row only to the order_items row for the exact same order and the exact same product.

USING is a shorthand when both tables share the same column names: USING (a, b) expands to ON T1.a = T2.a AND T1.b = T2.b. Since order_items and shipments both use order_id and product_id, that same join can be written FROM order_items JOIN shipments USING (order_id, product_id).

blocks.code:
-- ON form: two equality tests combined with AND
SELECT oi.order_id, oi.product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  ON oi.order_id = s.order_id
 AND oi.product_id = s.product_id;

-- USING form: shorthand when column names match on both sides
SELECT order_id, product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  USING (order_id, product_id);

annotations.text: ON with AND: both order_id AND product_id must match
USING: shorthand — expands to the same two-column condition

public.prompt: You are joining `order_items` to `shipments`. A row should only match when **both** `order_id` and `product_id` are equal. Which ON clause correctly expresses this two-column condition using `AND`?

options.text: ON order_items.order_id = shipments.order_id
ON order_items.order_id = shipments.order_id AND order_items.product_id = shipments.product_id
ON order_items.order_id = shipments.order_id OR order_items.product_id = shipments.product_id
ON order_items.order_id = shipments.product_id AND order_items.product_id = shipments.order_id

opt_a.message: This only checks order_id. A row from order_items could match a shipment row that shares the order_id but has a different product_id — that is a false match.

opt_b.message: Correct. The ON clause is a boolean expression, so you can chain equality tests with AND to require all columns to match simultaneously.

opt_c.message: OR would match whenever either column agrees, which allows false matches — a row where only order_id matches would still join.

opt_d.message: The columns are crossed: order_id is compared to product_id and vice versa. Each column must be matched to its counterpart: order_id = order_id AND product_id = product_id.

correct.message: The ON clause accepts any boolean expression, so you can combine multiple equality tests with AND to require all columns to match.

incorrect.message: To require two columns to match simultaneously, combine two equality tests with AND inside the ON clause.

hints: The ON clause works like a WHERE clause — you can use AND to combine conditions.
Each condition should compare one column from the left table to the corresponding column on the right.

public.prompt:
The query below uses a two-column ON clause:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM order_items
JOIN shipments ON order_items.order_id = shipments.order_id
               AND order_items.product_id = shipments.product_id;
```

Both tables share the column names `order_id` and `product_id`. Which USING clause is the correct shorthand?

options.text: USING (order_id, product_id)
USING order_id AND product_id
USING (order_id) AND USING (product_id)
USING order_id = shipments.order_id AND product_id = shipments.product_id

opt_a.message: Correct. USING (a, b) is the shorthand for ON T1.a = T2.a AND T1.b = T2.b when both tables share those column names.

opt_b.message: USING requires a parenthesised column list, not bare column names joined with AND. The correct form is USING (order_id, product_id).

opt_c.message: There is only one USING clause per join. List all shared columns inside a single pair of parentheses: USING (order_id, product_id).

opt_d.message: USING takes only column names, not equality expressions. The equality is implied by the shared name. Write USING (order_id, product_id).

correct.message: USING (a, b) is a compact shorthand: it forms the join condition ON T1.a = T2.a AND T1.b = T2.b automatically, as long as both tables share those column names.

incorrect.message: USING takes a parenthesised list of shared column names. All columns go inside one pair of parentheses, separated by commas.

hints: USING requires parentheses around the column list.
You only need to list the column names — the equality is implied because both tables share the same name.

steps.title: Join order_items to shipments on two keys

public.prompt: The `order_items` and `shipments` tables both have `order_id` and `product_id` columns. A shipment matches a line item only when **both** columns agree. Write a query that joins `order_items` to `shipments` using an ON clause with AND, and returns **order_id**, **product_id**, **quantity**, **unit_price**, and **shipped_date**, ordered by `order_id` then `product_id`.

files.content:
-- order_items columns: order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price
-- shipments columns: order_id, product_id, shipped_date
-- Join on BOTH order_id AND product_id.
-- Return: order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, shipped_date
-- ordered by order_id, product_id.

allowed_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
blocked_syntax: subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT oi.order_id, oi.product_id, oi.quantity, oi.unit_price, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id
ORDER BY oi.order_id, oi.product_id;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return only rows where both order_id and product_id match. Check that your ON clause uses AND to combine both conditions.

correct.message: Your ON clause with AND correctly requires both order_id and product_id to match. Rows that share only one of the two columns are excluded.

incorrect.message: Make sure your ON clause checks both order_id AND product_id. A single-column condition would allow false matches.

hints: The ON clause is a boolean expression — use AND to chain two equality tests.
Qualify each column with its table alias to avoid ambiguity: `oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id`.

steps.title: Keeping unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN
steps.lede: An inner join drops customers with no orders. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, filling missing order columns with NULL.

blocks.text: An inner join between customers and orders drops any customer with zero orders. To list every customer — including those who haven't ordered yet — you need an outer join.

A LEFT OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds a row for each row of T1 with no match in T2, filling T2's columns with NULL. SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id lists every customer; delivery_time_minutes is NULL for any customer with no orders.

blocks.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN
blocks.alt_text: LEFT JOIN: customer_id=1 matches order 1001 normally. Customers 4 and 5 have no orders — they appear in the result with NULL in the delivery_time_minutes column. An INNER JOIN would have dropped them entirely.

steps.title: RIGHT, FULL, and the optional OUTER keyword
steps.lede: LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row. RIGHT and FULL extend that logic to the other side or both sides.

blocks.text: A RIGHT OUTER JOIN is the converse of a left join: it keeps every row of T2, NULL-filling T1's columns for rows of T2 with no match. A FULL OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds NULL-filled rows for the unmatched rows of both T1 and T2 — so no row from either table is lost.
INNER and OUTER are both optional keywords. LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each already imply an outer join even without writing OUTER, so LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN mean exactly the same thing.

segments.label: LEFT JOIN on customers and orders: customers without orders appear with NULLs
segments.summary: Sets the task of listing customers with their orders, including customers who placed none, then reruns the inner-join query as a LEFT JOIN. A row-by-row walkthrough treats customers as the left table because it comes first after FROM: matched customers show their order data, and a customer with no orders still appears with NULLs on the right-hand side.

segments.label: FULL, LEFT and RIGHT OUTER JOIN on employee demographics and salary tables
segments.summary: Changes an earlier inner join of employee demographics and salary tables into a FULL OUTER JOIN. An employee with no salary row appears with NULLs, and the reverse for unmatched salary rows, and a Venn picture shows everything from both tables. It then switches to LEFT OUTER JOIN, which keeps everything from the first table plus the overlap, and to RIGHT, described as the exact opposite.

steps.title: LEFT JOIN and choosing RIGHT or FULL

public.prompt: You want a result that lists **every customer**, including those with no orders, with `NULL` in the order columns for customers who have not ordered. Which join type achieves this without adding extra rows for unmatched orders, when customers is the left table?

options.text: INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
FULL JOIN

opt_a.message: An INNER JOIN drops customers with no orders. You would lose any customer who has not placed an order yet.

opt_b.message: Correct. A LEFT JOIN performs an inner join and then adds a row for each left-table row with no match, filling the right-table columns with NULL. Every customer appears at least once.

opt_c.message: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table (orders here), not every customer. Customers with no orders would still be dropped.

opt_d.message: A FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. That would also add rows for orders with no matching customer — more than you need here.

correct.message: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table (customers) and fills the right-table columns with NULL for any customer with no matching order.

incorrect.message: Think about which table you want to preserve completely. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, filling NULLs for unmatched right-table columns.

hints: An INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows from both sides. You need a join that keeps unmatched rows from one side.
The 'left' in LEFT JOIN refers to the table written first — after FROM.

public.prompt: A colleague writes `LEFT OUTER JOIN`. Another writes `LEFT JOIN`. What is the relationship between these two forms?

options.text: They are identical — OUTER is optional and changes nothing
LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps more rows than LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN is shorthand for LEFT INNER JOIN, which is different
OUTER is required; omitting it makes LEFT JOIN behave like INNER JOIN

opt_a.message: Correct. INNER and OUTER are both optional keywords. LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each already imply an outer join, so LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are exactly the same.

opt_b.message: The two forms are identical. Adding or removing OUTER does not change the number of rows returned.

opt_c.message: There is no LEFT INNER JOIN. LEFT already implies outer. Writing LEFT JOIN alone means LEFT OUTER JOIN.

opt_d.message: OUTER is optional, not required. LEFT JOIN without OUTER still performs a left outer join — it does not become an inner join.

correct.message: OUTER is an optional keyword. LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each imply an outer join on their own, so the word OUTER adds no new meaning.

incorrect.message: Remember: INNER and OUTER are both optional. LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are exactly the same operation.

hints: Think about what the word OUTER adds — does removing it change which rows are kept?
The glossary states that LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each imply an outer join even without writing OUTER.

steps.title: Write a LEFT JOIN to keep all customers

public.prompt: Write a query that lists **every customer** along with their orders, including customers who have placed no orders. Return **customer_id**, **name**, **order_id**, and **delivery_time_minutes**, ordered by `customer_id` then `order_id`. Customers with no orders should appear with `NULL` in the order columns.

files.content:
-- customers columns: customer_id, name, city
-- orders columns: order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes, order_date, region, amount, city
-- Use LEFT JOIN so every customer appears even with no orders.
-- Return: customer_id, name, order_id, delivery_time_minutes
-- ordered by customer_id, order_id.

allowed_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
blocked_syntax: subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.delivery_time_minutes
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return every customer at least once, with NULL in order columns for customers who have no orders. Check that you are using LEFT JOIN and ordering by customer_id then order_id.

correct.message: Your LEFT JOIN correctly keeps every customer. Customers 4, 5, and 6 appear with NULL order columns because they have no matching orders.

incorrect.message: Make sure you use LEFT JOIN (not INNER JOIN) so that customers with no orders still appear. Check your ORDER BY clause too.

hints: Put customers first (after FROM) so it is the 'left' table — LEFT JOIN then keeps every customer row.
Customers with no orders will have NULL for order_id and delivery_time_minutes in the result.

steps.title: Joins: what you've learned
steps.lede: Three join patterns cover most real-world needs.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides. Extend ON with AND to match on multiple columns, or use USING when the column names are identical. LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row and NULL-fills the right side for unmatched rows; RIGHT and FULL extend that logic. OUTER is always optional.

blocks.title: Up next: Query Execution Order
blocks.text: SQL clauses are written in one order but processed in another — FROM first, SELECT last. Next you'll trace that order and learn where aliases can and cannot be used.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows survive: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare what an INNER JOIN keeps versus what it drops.

blocks.text: customers has six rows (customer_id 1–6). orders has rows for customer_id 1, 2, and 3 only. An INNER JOIN ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id produces rows only for customers 1, 2, and 3 — the ones with at least one matching order. Customers 4, 5, and 6 have no matching order row, so they are dropped entirely from the result. The rule: a row survives only if both sides have a match.

remediation_steps.title: Extending ON with AND: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: See what changes when you add a second condition to ON.

blocks.text: Single-column join: FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id — this matches every shipment for the same order, even if the product_id differs. Composite join: ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id — now both columns must agree. Only the shipment for the exact same order and the exact same product is joined. The ON clause accepts any boolean expression, so AND works the same way it does in WHERE.

remediation_steps.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same query with JOIN versus LEFT JOIN gives very different row counts.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN: SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id — returns only customers 1, 2, and 3, who have orders. Customers 4, 5, and 6 are dropped. LEFT JOIN: replace JOIN with LEFT JOIN — now all six customers appear. Customers 4, 5, and 6 get a row with delivery_time_minutes = NULL. The left table (customers) always contributes at least one row to the result.
